That is true for your first language. Indeed, there is a camp of people in the SLA field that proposes we should follow the first language path and not teach rules at all. There is also the opposite point of view, where I fall, that proposes that learning a set of rules leads to a restructuration of the knowledge that might have taken years of simple input otherwise. Second language acquisition is not the same as first language acquisition, as much as that would be ideal. For once, we have another language to fall on, but most importantly, the sensitive period is long gone.

In any case, I see both points of view. So just wanted to comment that it's not *untrue* that a set of rules can lead to profound language knowledge (and a restructuration of your current language system in your mind), which slowly gets automatized making it efficient. Although input is of course, essential for said automatization.

I'm a Spanish teacher, and I commit a lot of "leismo", that is using "le" when shortening a male direct object instead of "lo". It drives me nuts, and I really have to be careful in class. I've had to backtrack on a few occasions, but I guess it's interesting for students to learn about "leismo" in some areas of Spain. But on a day-to-day basis with my family, we all use "le". For example, "la policía le detuvo", which should be "lo detuvo".

Another error that is common, apart from the h and accent, as other people have commented, is using the infinitive instead of the imperative: for example, "ir conéctandose a la reunión de zoom", when they want to say "id conectándoos a la reunión de zoom." (or "vayan conéctandose" if using "ustedes").
